description: What is machine learning, in one sentence?
explanation: Machine learning builds models that learn patterns from examples rather than being given explicit rules for every case.
choice0: Any program that runs automatically without a user
choice1: Building models that learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules
choice2: Storing very large amounts of data efficiently
choice3: A faster way of writing ordinary computer programs

description: What is a feature in a machine learning dataset?
explanation: A feature is one input variable describing each example, such as a houses floor area.
choice0: An input variable describing each example
choice1: The answer the model is trying to predict
choice2: A bug in the training process
choice3: The name of the algorithm being used

description: What is the label in a supervised learning dataset?
explanation: The label is the known correct answer attached to each training example, which the model learns to predict.
choice0: The name of the dataset
choice1: A tag describing which algorithm to use
choice2: The known correct answer for each example
choice3: The row number of each example

description: What makes learning supervised?
explanation: Supervised learning trains on examples that already carry the correct answer.
choice0: A human watches the training process
choice1: The model is checked by a second model
choice2: The data is collected manually
choice3: Every training example comes with a known correct answer

description: What makes learning unsupervised?
explanation: Unsupervised learning works on data with no labels, looking for structure such as groups or patterns.
choice0: There are no labels, so the model looks for structure in the data
choice1: Nobody checks the results
choice2: The model trains without a computer
choice3: The data has no missing values

description: What kind of problem is predicting whether an email is spam or not spam?
explanation: Predicting which of a fixed set of categories something belongs to is classification.
choice0: Regression
choice1: Classification
choice2: Clustering
choice3: Dimensionality reduction

description: What kind of problem is predicting the price of a house?
explanation: Predicting a continuous numeric value is regression.
choice0: Regression
choice1: Classification
choice2: Clustering
choice3: Anomaly detection

description: What kind of problem is grouping customers into segments with no predefined categories?
explanation: Discovering groups in unlabelled data is clustering, an unsupervised task.
choice0: Regression
choice1: Classification
choice2: Clustering
choice3: Forecasting a label

description: What is the difference between classification and regression?
explanation: Classification predicts a category, while regression predicts a continuous number.
choice0: Classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number
choice1: Classification predicts a number, regression predicts a category
choice2: Classification is supervised, regression is unsupervised
choice3: They are two names for the same task

description: Which of these is an unsupervised task?
explanation: Clustering finds structure without labels. The others all learn from known answers.
choice0: Predicting tomorrows temperature from past weather
choice1: Deciding whether a transaction is fraudulent from labelled examples
choice2: Predicting exam scores from study hours
choice3: Grouping news articles by topic with no topics given in advance

description: What is a training set?
explanation: The training set is the portion of the data the model learns from.
choice0: The data the model learns from
choice1: The data used to measure final performance
choice2: The data that was discarded as unusable
choice3: The list of settings used by the algorithm

description: What is a test set?
explanation: The test set is data held back from training and used once, to estimate how the model will do on new data.
choice0: Extra data added to make training faster
choice1: Data held back from training, used to estimate performance on new data
choice2: The subset of features that matter most
choice3: A copy of the training data

description: Why must the test set be kept separate from training?
explanation: A model can score well on data it has already seen, so testing on training data tells you nothing about new cases.
choice0: To make training run faster
choice1: To reduce the size of the dataset
choice2: Because scoring on data the model has already seen says nothing about new data
choice3: Because test data is usually of poorer quality

description: What is a row in a typical machine learning dataset usually called?
explanation: Each row is one example, also called an observation, instance or sample.
choice0: An example, or observation
choice1: A feature
choice2: A label
choice3: A parameter

description: What does it mean for a dataset to be labelled?
explanation: A labelled dataset carries the correct answer for each example, which is what supervised learning needs.
choice0: It has column names
choice1: It has been sorted into order
choice2: It has been checked for errors
choice3: Each example carries its correct answer

description: What is overfitting?
explanation: An overfit model has learned the noise and quirks of the training data, so it does well there and badly on new data.
choice0: The model is too simple to capture the pattern
choice1: The model has learned the training data too closely and generalises badly
choice2: The dataset has too many rows
choice3: The model takes too long to train

description: What is underfitting?
explanation: An underfit model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it performs poorly even on training data.
choice0: The model is too simple and performs poorly even on training data
choice1: The model memorises the training data
choice2: The dataset has too few columns
choice3: The model was trained for too long

description: A model scores 99 percent on training data and 62 percent on unseen data. What is happening?
explanation: A large gap between training and unseen performance is the classic signature of overfitting.
hint: Compare the two scores rather than looking at either alone.
choice0: Underfitting
choice1: Overfitting
choice2: The test set is too large
choice3: The model needs more features

description: A model scores 61 percent on training data and 60 percent on unseen data. What is happening?
explanation: Poor performance on both sets, with little gap, points to a model too simple for the problem.
choice0: Overfitting
choice1: The data leaked between the sets
choice2: Underfitting
choice3: The model is performing well

description: What does it mean for a model to generalise well?
explanation: Generalising well means performing accurately on new data it has never seen, not just on its training examples.
choice0: It performs well on new data it has never seen
choice1: It runs on many kinds of computer
choice2: It can be applied to any dataset without retraining
choice3: It uses very few features

description: What does accuracy measure?
explanation: Accuracy is the share of predictions that were correct out of all predictions made.
choice0: How close the predictions are to the average
choice1: How quickly the model produces a prediction
choice2: How many features the model uses
choice3: The share of predictions that were correct

description: Why can a model with 99 percent accuracy still be useless?
explanation: If 99 percent of cases are one class, always guessing that class scores 99 percent while never catching the cases you care about.
hint: Think about what always guessing the common answer would score.
choice0: If one class is very rare, always guessing the common class scores highly while catching nothing
choice1: Accuracy above 95 percent is always a calculation error
choice2: Accuracy cannot be measured on a test set
choice3: Because accuracy ignores the training data

description: What is a baseline in model evaluation?
explanation: A baseline is a deliberately simple reference, such as always predicting the most common class, that a real model must beat.
choice0: The lowest score the model reached during training
choice1: A simple reference result the real model must beat
choice2: The first row of the dataset
choice3: The score on the training set

description: Roughly what order do the steps of a machine learning project take?
explanation: You gather and prepare the data, split it, train on the training portion, then evaluate on held-out data.
choice0: Train, gather data, evaluate, split
choice1: Evaluate, train, gather data, split
choice2: Gather and prepare data, split it, train, evaluate
choice3: Split, evaluate, gather data, train

description: Why is data preparation usually the largest part of a project?
explanation: Real data arrives messy, inconsistent and incomplete, and models can only be as good as the data they are given.
choice0: Real data is messy and incomplete, and model quality depends on it
choice1: Because algorithms take only seconds to write
choice2: Because datasets must always be sorted first
choice3: Because preparation must be redone for every prediction

description: What is a common problem with missing values in a dataset?
explanation: Many algorithms cannot handle gaps, and how you fill them can bias the result, so missing data must be handled deliberately.
choice0: They make the file larger
choice1: Many algorithms cannot handle them, and filling them carelessly biases results
choice2: They always mean the row is invalid
choice3: They prevent the data from being sorted

description: What is an outlier?
explanation: An outlier is a value far away from the rest, which may be a genuine rare case or a data error.
choice0: A value that appears most often
choice1: A row with a missing label
choice2: The average of the extreme values
choice3: A value far away from the rest of the data

description: Why does the amount of training data usually matter?
explanation: More varied examples give the model more chance to learn the real pattern rather than the quirks of a few cases.
choice0: More varied examples help the model learn the real pattern rather than quirks
choice1: More data always makes training faster
choice2: More data removes the need for a test set
choice3: More data guarantees perfect accuracy

description: What is a model, in machine learning terms?
explanation: A model is what the learning process produces: a rule or function that turns inputs into a prediction.
choice0: The dataset used for training
choice1: The programming language used
choice2: What training produces: a function mapping inputs to predictions
choice3: A diagram of the project plan

description: What does training a model actually do?
explanation: Training adjusts the models internal settings so its predictions match the training examples as closely as possible.
choice0: Adjusts the models settings so its predictions fit the training examples
choice1: Copies the training data into the model
choice2: Sorts the data into the right order
choice3: Chooses which programming language to use

description: What is prediction, or inference?
explanation: Prediction is using a trained model on new input to produce an output.
choice0: Retraining the model on new data
choice1: Using a trained model on new input to produce an output
choice2: Measuring how accurate the model is
choice3: Choosing which features to keep

description: What does a decision tree do?
explanation: A decision tree splits the data with a sequence of yes or no questions, and each leaf gives a prediction.
choice0: Splits data with a series of yes or no questions leading to a prediction
choice1: Draws a family tree of the dataset
choice2: Sorts the data alphabetically
choice3: Connects every example to its nearest neighbour

description: What is the core idea of the k-nearest-neighbours method?
explanation: It predicts for a new point by looking at the most similar examples it has already seen.
choice0: It fits a straight line through the data
choice1: It splits data into two halves repeatedly
choice2: It always predicts the average value
choice3: It predicts using the most similar examples already seen

description: What does linear regression fit to the data?
explanation: Linear regression fits a straight-line relationship between the inputs and a numeric output.
choice0: A set of yes or no rules
choice1: A straight-line relationship between inputs and a numeric output
choice2: A grouping of similar points
choice3: A ranking of the features

description: Despite its name, what does logistic regression predict?
explanation: Logistic regression is a classification method: it predicts the probability of belonging to a class.
choice0: A continuous number
choice1: A cluster assignment
choice2: The probability of belonging to a class
choice3: The number of features to keep

description: What is a neural network, in simple terms?
explanation: A neural network passes inputs through layers of simple connected units, each layer building on the last.
choice0: Layers of simple connected units that transform the input step by step
choice1: A network of computers sharing one dataset
choice2: A diagram showing how features relate
choice3: A method for storing data efficiently

description: How does deep learning relate to machine learning?
explanation: Deep learning is a branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers.
choice0: They are unrelated fields
choice1: Deep learning is machine learning using neural networks with many layers
choice2: Machine learning is a branch of deep learning
choice3: Deep learning refers to training on very large computers

description: Where does bias in a machine learning model usually come from?
explanation: A model reproduces the patterns in its training data, so historical bias in that data comes out in its predictions.
choice0: Patterns in the training data, which the model reproduces
choice1: Random errors during training
choice2: Using too many features
choice3: Running the model on the wrong computer

description: Why does it matter whether a model can be explained?
explanation: When a decision affects people, being able to say why the model decided as it did is needed for trust, appeal and accountability.
choice0: Because explainable models are always more accurate
choice1: Because it makes training faster
choice2: Because decisions affecting people need to be justifiable and challengeable
choice3: Because it reduces the amount of data needed

description: What is a reasonable response to a model that performs worse for one group of people?
explanation: Measure performance separately for each group and address the gap, rather than relying on the overall average.
choice0: Ignore it if overall accuracy is high
choice1: Remove that group from the test set
choice2: Raise the decision threshold for everyone
choice3: Measure performance per group and work to close the gap

description: What is a prediction error, or residual, in regression?
explanation: It is the difference between what the model predicted and what actually happened.
choice0: The gap between the predicted value and the actual value
choice1: The number of rows the model could not process
choice2: The time taken to make a prediction
choice3: The share of features that were unused

description: Why should the split into training and test data usually be random?
explanation: A random split makes both parts representative. Splitting by position can put all of one kind of case on one side.
choice0: Because random numbers make models more accurate
choice1: So both parts are representative rather than sorted into unlike groups
choice2: Because it is faster than splitting in order
choice3: Because it removes duplicate rows

description: What is a hyperparameter?
explanation: A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training, such as how deep a tree may grow, rather than something learned from data.
choice0: A value the model learns from the data
choice1: A feature with unusually large values
choice2: A setting chosen before training rather than learned from data
choice3: The final accuracy score

description: What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?
explanation: Parameters are learned during training; hyperparameters are set beforehand to control how training happens.
choice0: Parameters are learned from data, hyperparameters are chosen beforehand
choice1: Parameters are chosen beforehand, hyperparameters are learned
choice2: They are the same thing
choice3: Parameters apply to classification, hyperparameters to regression

description: What is anomaly detection used for?
explanation: Anomaly detection flags examples that look unlike the normal pattern, such as possible fraud or equipment faults.
choice0: Grouping similar customers together
choice1: Flagging examples that look unlike the usual pattern
choice2: Predicting a continuous value
choice3: Reducing the number of features

description: What is a recommendation system trying to do?
explanation: It predicts which items a person is likely to want, from their behaviour and that of similar people.
choice0: Predict which items a person is likely to want
choice1: Sort a catalogue alphabetically
choice2: Detect errors in a product database
choice3: Compress a large dataset

description: Why is it a mistake to judge a model only on its training score?
explanation: The training score reflects data the model has already seen, so it flatters the model and hides overfitting.
choice0: Because training scores are always low
choice1: Because the training set is usually too small
choice2: Because training scores cannot be calculated for classifiers
choice3: Because it reflects data the model has already seen and hides overfitting

description: What does it mean for classes to be imbalanced?
explanation: One class appears far more often than another, which can make a model that ignores the rare class look good.
choice0: One class is far more common than the other
choice1: The features have very different units
choice2: The training and test sets are different sizes
choice3: Some rows have missing labels

description: Why is machine learning a poor fit for a problem with clear, stable rules?
explanation: When the rules are known and stable, writing them directly is simpler, more predictable and easier to check than learning them.
choice0: Because models cannot handle rules at all
choice1: Because rule-based problems always have too little data
choice2: Because writing the rules directly is simpler and easier to verify
choice3: Because models can only handle numeric data

description: What is the practical meaning of the phrase garbage in, garbage out?
explanation: A model trained on poor-quality data will produce poor predictions, however good the algorithm is.
choice0: Models should discard rows they cannot use
choice1: Poor input data produces poor predictions, whatever algorithm is used
choice2: Data should be deleted after training
choice3: Compressed data leads to compressed results
